problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（Distinction Between Informational and Persuasive Texts、Persuasive Writing Structure、Rhetorical Appeals (Pathos, Ethos, Logos)、Main Idea and Supporting Details）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

objective: Persuasive writing aims to output opinions and persuade readers, while informational texts present objective facts without a debatable claim.；A key distinction: persuasive texts have a debatable topic; informational texts simply state facts.；Persuasive writing can include factual information to support its argument.

learningGoals.statement: Distinguish between informational and persuasive texts based on the presence of a debatable claim.
Identify the essential structural components of a persuasive essay, including counterargument.
Recognize and differentiate rhetorical appeals (pathos, ethos, logos) in persuasive writing.
Demonstrate the ability to extract the main idea from an informational or persuasive text and distinguish it from supporting details.
Apply the convention of avoiding first-person pronouns in formal persuasive writing to maintain objectivity.

knowledgeNodes.name: Distinction Between Informational and Persuasive Texts
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Distinction Between Informational and Persuasive Texts
knowledgeNodes.definition: A text is persuasive if its topic is debatable and it seeks to output opinions and persuade the reader. Informational texts present objective facts without a debatable claim. Persuasive texts may contain factual information for support.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.

knowledgeNodes.name: Persuasive Writing Structure
knowledgeNodes.definition: A persuasive essay includes an introduction, clear claim, supporting evidence, and a counterargument. Maintain objectivity and cite authoritative sources. Avoid first-person language.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

knowledgeNodes.name: Rhetorical Appeals (Pathos, Ethos, Logos)
knowledgeNodes.definition: Three main rhetorical appeals: pathos appeals to emotions, ethos establishes credibility and ethics, logos uses logic and reasoning.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.

knowledgeNodes.name: Main Idea and Supporting Details
knowledgeNodes.definition: Identify the central claim of a text and classify supporting details. This involves distinguishing the overarching argument from evidence.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.

knowledgeNodes.name: Avoiding First-Person in Persuasive Writing
knowledgeNodes.definition: In formal persuasive writing, avoid subjective expressions like 'I think' or 'I believe'. Present arguments objectively to maintain credibility.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

questions.stem: Read the following short passage and decide whether it is an informational or persuasive text: 'Pompeii was an ancient Roman city buried under volcanic ash after Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD. The ash preserved buildings, artifacts, and even human remains, giving archaeologists a unique glimpse into daily life.'
questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies the passage as informational because it presents objective facts without a debatable claim.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
questions.alignmentNote: This expectation covers understanding text types, which is directly assessed by distinguishing informational from persuasive texts.
questions.stemIntent: Determine whether the student can distinguish informational from persuasive texts based on the absence of a debatable claim.
questions.commonMisconception: Believing that any text containing facts is automatically informational, ignoring whether it also presents a debatable opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: Informational, because it only presents facts about Pompeii without arguing a position.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! The text provides objective facts and does not try to persuade the reader of a debatable point.

options.label: B
options.text: Persuasive, because it contains historical information.
options.feedbackWrong: Historical information alone does not make a text persuasive. The key is whether the text takes a stance on a debatable topic.

options.label: C
options.text: Informational, because all paragraphs about history are informational.
options.feedbackWrong: A history text could be persuasive if it argues a particular interpretation. Here, there is no argument, just facts.

options.label: D
options.text: Persuasive, because it tries to convince readers that Pompeii is interesting.
options.feedbackWrong: The passage does not explicitly try to convince; it merely reports what happened. Look for a clear claim or opinion.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers a diagnostic question targeting err-distinction-misclassify incorrectly.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Confusing informational and persuasive texts by believing any text with facts is automatically informational, ignoring the presence of a debatable thesis.

miniLesson.explain: A persuasive text does more than state facts; it takes a side on a debatable issue. Informational texts present objective facts without a debatable claim. Even if a persuasive text contains factual information, it remains persuasive because its purpose is to convince the reader of a particular opinion. To classify a text, ask: 'Is the author arguing a debatable point?' If yes, it's persuasive. If the text simply reports facts without trying to persuade, it's informational.
miniLesson.example: Consider two Pompeii texts: Text A describes the eruption and preserved ruins purely with facts. Text B argues that Pompeii is a better travel destination than Rome because it offers better value. Text A is informational; Text B is persuasive because it compares and argues a debatable preference.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Ask: 'Is there a debatable claim?' Yes → persuasive; No → informational.

guidedPractice.prompt: Classify the following sentence as informational or persuasive: 'Pompeii was buried under volcanic ash after Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD.'
guidedPractice.answer: Informational, because it states a fact without a debatable claim.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read both sentences: A: 'Pompeii contains well-preserved Roman ruins.' B: 'Pompeii is a better travel destination than Rome because it offers a unique look at ancient life.' Which sentence is persuasive?
guidedPractice.answer: Sentence B is persuasive because it makes a debatable comparison and argument.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this short paragraph: 'Pompeii attracts many tourists each year. The ruins are precious and must be protected. The government should limit visitor numbers.' Is it informational or persuasive? Explain your reasoning.
guidedPractice.answer: Persuasive, because even though it includes factual statements, it argues a debatable position that the government should limit visitors.

reteachModules.trigger: The student omits the counterargument section when writing or outlining a persuasive essay.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that a persuasive essay only needs an introduction, claim, and supporting evidence; they do not realize that addressing and refuting a counterargument is a required structural component.

miniLesson.explain: A standard persuasive essay has four parts: introduction, clear claim, supporting evidence, and counterargument. The counterargument shows that you understand the opposing view and can refute it, making your argument stronger and more logical. Without it, the essay is one-sided and less credible.
miniLesson.example: Using the Pompeii example, if you write a persuasive text arguing that Pompeii is the better travel destination because it offers better value, you must also address why a competing destination might appeal to some travellers and then explain why Pompeii still wins. That is the counterargument.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: I.C.E.C. — Introduce, Claim, Evidence, Counterargument. Don't forget the final C.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify the missing component in this persuasive essay structure: 1) Introduction, 2) Clear claim, 3) Supporting evidence, 4) ?

You are writing a persuasive essay on a topic from the lesson (e.g., e-sports in the Olympics). After presenting two body paragraphs of supporting evidence for your claim, what section should you add to strengthen your argument before writing the conclusion?
guidedPractice.answer: A counterargument section that acknowledges an opposing viewpoint and then refutes it.

guidedPractice.prompt: Here is an outline: Introduction with thesis, Body paragraph 1: evidence, Body paragraph 2: evidence, Conclusion. Identify the structural flaw and rewrite the outline to follow the standard persuasive essay structure.
guidedPractice.answer: The outline is missing a counterargument. Rewritten: Introduction with thesis, Body paragraph 1: evidence, Body paragraph 2: evidence, Counterargument, Conclusion.

reteachModules.trigger: Misidentifying rhetorical appeals, especially confusing ethos with logos or using emotional appeals when logical appeals are needed.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses the three rhetorical appeals: pathos (emotion), ethos (credibility/ethics), and logos (logic/reason). They may label a statement that appeals to authority as logical, or use an emotional story when concrete evidence is required.

miniLesson.explain: Remember: pathos appeals to emotion, ethos to credibility or ethics, and logos to logical reasoning. When you see statistics, evidence, and factual reasoning, that's logos. When an author mentions their expertise, qualifications, or moral character to build trust, that's ethos. When a description provokes feelings such as pity, fear, or happiness, that's pathos. Ask yourself: 'Does this make me feel, trust, or think?'
miniLesson.example: A persuasive paragraph about public transit: 'Public transit reduced commute times by 25% in our city last year.' This is logos because it gives a measurable statistic. 'As a transportation engineer with 15 years of experience, I recommend expanding the bus network.' This is ethos because it relies on the author's expertise. 'Imagine a single mother missing her night shift because the last bus left early' is pathos because it evokes sympathy.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Ethos = Expert, Pathos = Passion, Logos = Logic (E-P-L).

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify the rhetorical appeal in this sentence: 'According to a peer-reviewed study, daily exercise reduces the risk of heart disease by 30%.'
guidedPractice.answer: Logos (logical appeal), because it cites a research study and uses a statistic.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following statements uses ethos? Choose A, B, or C.
A) 'Every year, thousands of animals are left homeless after natural disasters.'
B) 'As a wildlife biologist who has studied habitat loss for a decade, I urge you to protect these lands.'
C) 'If we cut funding for parks, the city will lose more than $2 million in tourism revenue.'
guidedPractice.answer: B. It establishes the speaker's credibility (ethos) by referencing their expertise as a wildlife biologist.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student's persuasive paragraph says: 'I think recycling is important because I feel sad when I see trash in the ocean. Just imagine the poor turtles crying for help.' Identify the rhetorical misapplication and rewrite the sentence using logos instead.
guidedPractice.answer: The student uses pathos (emotional appeal) and first-person subjective language. A logical rewrite: 'Recycling reduces the amount of plastic entering the ocean by up to 80%, according to environmental agencies, and each ton of plastic recycled prevents six tons of carbon emissions.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student identifies a supporting detail as the main idea when asked to summarize a passage.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student mistakes a specific fact or piece of evidence for the central claim, focusing on a single detail instead of the overall message.

miniLesson.explain: The main idea is the most important point a text makes. It is the big umbrella that covers all the details. Supporting details are the specific facts, examples, or statistics that explain, prove, or elaborate the main idea. To find the main idea, ask: 'What is this mostly about?' not 'What one fact does it mention?'
miniLesson.example: In the passage 'Regular exercise provides numerous health benefits. Studies show it reduces the risk of heart disease, improves mental health, and helps maintain a healthy weight. Incorporating just 30 minutes of walking each day can significantly increase overall well-being,' the main idea is that regular exercise has many health benefits. The mention of heart disease, mental health, or 30 minutes of walking are supporting details.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Imagine the main idea is the headline of a newspaper article, and supporting details are the facts in the story below it. The headline sums it all up.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify the main idea: 'Volcanoes can be destructive. For example, Mount Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii, and Mount St. Helens caused massive damage.'
guidedPractice.answer: The main idea is that volcanoes can be destructive.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read: 'Regular exercise provides numerous health benefits. Studies show it reduces the risk of heart disease, improves mental health, and helps maintain a healthy weight. Incorporating just 30 minutes of walking each day can significantly increase overall well-being.' Write the main idea and list one supporting detail.
guidedPractice.answer: Main idea: Regular exercise has many health benefits. Supporting detail: It reduces the risk of heart disease.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following short text: 'Persuasive writing aims to persuade readers by using a debatable claim, while informational texts present objective facts. Persuasive writing often includes factual evidence, but it always has a clear position. For example, a text about Pompeii that compares travel destinations for cost-effectiveness is persuasive, while one simply describing the city is informational.' Identify the main idea and explain why 'a text about Pompeii that compares travel destinations' is not the main idea.
guidedPractice.answer: Main idea: The distinction between persuasive and informational texts depends on the presence of a debatable claim. The Pompeii comparison is a supporting example, not the central claim.

reteachModules.trigger: Student uses first-person pronouns (I, we, my, our) in formal persuasive writing or selects a first-person sentence as acceptable in a persuasive text.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that phrases like 'I think' make their argument more personal and persuasive, or does not recognize that first-person language weakens objectivity and credibility in formal persuasive writing.

miniLesson.explain: In formal persuasive writing, your goal is to convince readers through logic and evidence, not through personal feelings. Using 'I think' or 'I believe' shifts focus to the writer's personal opinion and makes the argument feel subjective. Instead, state your claim directly and support it with authoritative sources. This maintains a logical, objective tone and strengthens ethos, your credibility as a writer.
miniLesson.example: Weak: 'I think e-sports should be included in the Olympics because they require skill.' Strong: 'E-sports should be included in the Olympics because they demand strategic thinking, precise teamwork, and rigorous training, as shown by competitive gaming statistics.' Notice how the revised version removes first-person and lets the evidence carry the argument.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: No 'I' in objective — if you see 'I think,' delete it. Persuasive power comes from proof, not pronouns.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which sentence is NOT appropriate for a formal persuasive essay because it uses first-person language? A) Investment in public transit reduces traffic congestion. B) I feel that public transit investment is necessary. C) Studies show that public transit investment lowers emissions. D) A counterargument might mention the high upfront cost.
guidedPractice.answer: B) I feel that public transit investment is necessary.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following sentence to remove first-person and maintain an objective, persuasive tone: 'I believe the carbon tax is the best tool to reduce emissions.'
guidedPractice.answer: The carbon tax is an effective tool to reduce emissions, as supported by economic studies and expert analysis.

guidedPractice.prompt: Choose the sentence that best maintains objectivity in a persuasive paragraph about zoo animal ethics. A) In my opinion, zoos should be phased out. B) We must stop keeping animals in zoos. C) Scientific studies show that many zoo animals exhibit signs of stress, suggesting that traditional zoo environments may not fully meet animal welfare needs. D) I think zoos are unethical and cruel.
guidedPractice.answer: C) Scientific studies show that many zoo animals exhibit signs of stress, suggesting that traditional zoo environments may not fully meet animal welfare needs.

questions.stem: Which of the following texts is persuasive?
options: The Eiffel Tower is 330 meters tall and was completed in 1889.
The city should invest more in public transit because it reduces traffic and pollution.
Canada's population is approximately 38 million people.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Carbon taxes have been shown to lower emissions in several countries. These countries also report improved air quality. Therefore, our province should adopt a carbon tax.' Is this text informational or persuasive? Explain your answer using the idea of a debatable claim.
questions.rubric: The student must state that the text is persuasive because it contains a debatable claim (the province should adopt a carbon tax) and its purpose is to convince the reader, even though it includes factual supporting statements.

retestCards.passRule: Answer question 1 correctly (choose the persuasive text) and provide a response to question 2 that correctly identifies the text as persuasive and explains it has a debatable claim.

questions.stem: A student is outlining a persuasive essay arguing that public transit should receive more funding. The outline includes: Introduction, Claim, Supporting Evidence, Conclusion. Which essential component is missing?
options: Counterargument
Thesis statement
Background information
Works cited

questions.stem: You are writing a persuasive essay on whether zoos should be banned. Explain what a counterargument paragraph should do and why including it makes your argument stronger.
questions.rubric: Must acknowledge an opposing viewpoint and then refute it; must state that including a counterargument strengthens credibility or addresses reader objections.

retestCards.passRule: Answer question 1 correctly and provide an open-ended response that meets the rubric criteria.

questions.stem: Read this claim from an article arguing for a plastic bag ban: 'As a marine biologist with 20 years of experience studying ocean pollution, I have observed the devastating impact of plastic first-hand. Banning plastic bags is essential.' Which rhetorical appeal is primarily used?
options: Pathos (emotional appeal)
Ethos (credibility appeal)
Logos (logical appeal)
All three appeals equally

questions.stem: A classmate wrote this sentence in a persuasive essay about climate change: 'Just imagine the heartbreak of a polar bear losing its home because of melting ice. We must act now!' Identify the rhetorical appeal used, explain whether it is appropriate, and then rewrite the sentence to use logos instead.
questions.rubric: Correctly identifies pathos (emotional appeal). Explains that it is emotional and can be persuasive but lacks logical evidence. Provides a logical rewrite using specific evidence, statistics, or reasoning, such as 'Arctic sea ice has declined by 13% per decade, threatening polar bear habitats and forcing them to swim longer distances.'

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer Q1 correctly (ethos) and provide a response to Q2 that correctly identifies pathos, explains its persuasive role and limitation, and includes a logical rewrite with concrete evidence or reasoning.

questions.stem: Read the passage: 'Plastic pollution is one of the most serious environmental threats. Millions of tons of plastic enter the oceans each year, harming marine life. Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and many seabirds ingest plastic fragments. Reducing single-use plastics can help protect these animals.' What is the main idea?
options: Plastic pollution is a serious environmental threat.
Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.
Millions of tons of plastic enter the oceans each year.
Reducing single-use plastics can help protect animals.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'Sleep is essential for good health. It allows the body to repair itself, strengthens the immune system, and helps the brain form memories. Children and teenagers need about 9-10 hours of sleep per night, while adults need 7-8 hours.' Write the main idea of the passage, and then write one supporting detail that supports it.
questions.rubric: The main idea must express the overall point: sleep is essential for good health (or health requires adequate sleep). A supporting detail must be a specific fact from the passage, such as it allows the body to repair itself, strengthens the immune system, helps form memories, or the recommended hours for different age groups. The answer fails if the student lists only a detail as the main idea without identifying the broader claim.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be correct. For Q1, the student must select the correct main idea option. For Q2, the student must identify the main idea as the overall importance of sleep and give at least one accurate supporting detail from the passage.

questions.stem: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal persuasive essay about public transit?
options: I think that investing in public transit is important for reducing traffic.
In my opinion, public transit should be expanded in every major city.
Investing in public transit reduces traffic congestion and lowers greenhouse gas emissions, as shown by recent city reports.
We all know that public transit is better, so we need to fund it more.

questions.stem: Rewrite the following sentence to remove first-person language and make it more objective: 'I think that zoo animals should have more space and enrichment in their enclosures.'
questions.rubric: Response must eliminate all first-person pronouns (I, we, my, our, mine, us) and present a clear, objective claim. Example: 'Zoo animals should have more space and enrichment in their enclosures.' Or a sentence that states the claim directly without personal opinion, using evidence if possible.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the answer must contain no first-person pronouns and must present a clear, objective claim without using phrases like 'I think' or 'I believe'.

dashboardFormat.objective: Persuasive writing aims to output opinions and persuade readers, while informational texts present objective facts without a debatable claim.；A key distinction: persuasive texts have a debatable topic; informational texts simply state facts.；Persuasive writing can include factual information to support its argument.

learningGoals.statement: Distinguish between informational and persuasive texts based on the presence of a debatable claim.
Identify the essential structural components of a persuasive essay, including counterargument.
Recognize and differentiate rhetorical appeals (pathos, ethos, logos) in persuasive writing.
Demonstrate the ability to extract the main idea from an informational or persuasive text and distinguish it from supporting details.
Apply the convention of avoiding first-person pronouns in formal persuasive writing to maintain objectivity.

cards.question: Read the following short passage and decide whether it is an informational or persuasive text: 'Pompeii was an ancient Roman city buried under volcanic ash after Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD. The ash preserved buildings, artifacts, and even human remains, giving archaeologists a unique glimpse into daily life.'
options: Informational, because it only presents facts about Pompeii without arguing a position.
Persuasive, because it contains historical information.
Informational, because all paragraphs about history are informational.
Persuasive, because it tries to convince readers that Pompeii is interesting.
cards.diagnosis: Determine whether the student can distinguish informational from persuasive texts based on the absence of a debatable claim.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! The text provides objective facts and does not try to persuade the reader of a debatable point.
Historical information alone does not make a text persuasive. The key is whether the text takes a stance on a debatable topic.
A history text could be persuasive if it argues a particular interpretation. Here, there is no argument, just facts.
The passage does not explicitly try to convince; it merely reports what happened. Look for a clear claim or opinion.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies the passage as informational because it presents objective facts without a debatable claim.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
cards.alignmentNote: This expectation covers understanding text types, which is directly assessed by distinguishing informational from persuasive texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Believing that any text containing facts is automatically informational, ignoring whether it also presents a debatable opinion.

cards.question:
Which component is missing from the following partial persuasive essay outline? 
1. Introduction with thesis
2. Body paragraph 1: Evidence supporting claim
3. Body paragraph 2: More evidence
4. Conclusion
options: A title
A counterargument
A personal anecdote
A call to action
cards.diagnosis: Check if the student recognizes that a counterargument is a standard element of persuasive writing structure.
misconceptions: A title is helpful but not a structural requirement. The missing piece is a core argument component.
✓ Yes! A persuasive essay should address and refute opposing views to strengthen the argument.
A personal anecdote is optional and may even weaken objectivity. What’s missing is a key argumentative element.
A call to action is often in the conclusion, but the fundamental missing part is a counterargument section.
cards.successCriteria: Selects the counterargument as the missing element.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: This question assesses knowledge of the opinion piece (persuasive essay) structure, which falls under writing forms.
cards.commonMisconception: Omitting the counterargument, thinking that only supporting evidence is needed.

cards.question: Which of the following best illustrates the use of ethos in a persuasive piece?
options: Using statistics from a government report to support a claim.
Telling a heartwarming story about a family affected by the issue.
Citing the author’s 20 years of experience as a medical researcher.
Using a rhetorical question to make the reader think.
cards.diagnosis: Test the ability to recognize an ethos appeal based on credibility or ethical stance.
misconceptions: Statistics appeal to logic (logos), not ethics or credibility.
✓ Right! Emphasizing expertise and authority builds ethos, or credibility.
A rhetorical question can be a logical or emotional device, but it does not establish the author's credibility.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly links ethos to establishing credibility or ethical character.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the organizational structure and features of a variety of informational, narrative, and graphic texts, including information paragraphs, opinion pieces, textbooks, newspaper reports and magazine stories, and short fiction.
cards.alignmentNote: Rhetorical appeals are features of opinion pieces (persuasive texts), and understanding them aligns with the expectation of text features.
cards.commonMisconception: Confusing ethos with logos (logic) or pathos (emotion).

cards.question: Read the short passage and identify the main idea in one sentence: 'Regular exercise provides numerous health benefits. Studies show it reduces the risk of heart disease, improves mental health, and helps maintain a healthy weight. Incorporating just 30 minutes of walking each day can significantly increase overall well-being.'
cards.diagnosis: Assess whether the student can synthesize the overarching claim rather than repeating a supporting detail.
cards.successCriteria: States that the main idea is something like 'Exercise has many health benefits' or 'Regular exercise is very beneficial for health.'
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the content and meaning of informational, narrative, and graphic texts that they have read using a variety of reading strategies.
cards.alignmentNote: This expectation focuses on comprehending text meaning, including identifying the main idea.
cards.commonMisconception: Focusing on a specific detail (e.g., '30 minutes of walking') and mistaking it for the main idea.
